processing: Sun-dried raw maocha (or, in modern versions, ripe tea) is packed into a section of fresh fragrant bamboo, tamped down and roasted over embers in stages while more leaf is added, until the tea is compressed into a cylinder and the bamboo is charred; the tube is then split off or sold intact.
harvest_season: Made from spring or autumn maocha; traditionally a seasonal village product, now made year-round by small producers.
appearance_dry: A dense green-brown cylinder of leaf the diameter of a bamboo stalk, with the inner bamboo skin stuck to its surface, often sliced into thick coins; or the whole tube with charred outer skin.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to light amber for the raw version, red-brown for the ripe version, clear.
appearance_wet: Compressed layers of leaf peeling apart into whole, supple leaves that smell faintly of green bamboo.
taste_profile: Raw-tea honey and florals with a distinct sweet, grassy bamboo fragrance and a light toasty note from the roasting; ripe versions trade the florals for dates and earth under the same bamboo sweetness.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice; the cylinder is dense, so break off a coin and flake it along the layers. Water just off the boil; a longer first steep opens it. Ripe bamboo tea takes boiling water and a clay pot.

vintage_note: Sold by the year it was made and by whether the tea inside is raw or ripe, as whole tubes of 100–500 g or as sliced coins, mostly from small producers in Xishuangbanna and Pu'er and from a few Western vendors who commission it. Raw bamboo tea is drunk young (1–5 years) while the bamboo aroma is fresh, and it ages like loosely pressed sheng, slowly turning honeyed as the bamboo note fades; ripe bamboo tea is a 1–5-year product with no ageing tradition. The material inside is often ordinary plantation or young-tree leaf, so the year matters less than whether the roasting was done gently.
description:
Bamboo tube tea is a village tradition of southern Yunnan, associated with peoples such as the Bulang, Dai, Hani and Lahu: tea is packed into a fresh length of fragrant bamboo and roasted over a fire, in stages, until it is pressed into a solid cylinder that takes on the sweet green smell of the bamboo. It is both a way of storing tea and a flavour in its own right.

Traditionally the tea inside is sun-dried raw leaf, and that is still the classic version; many modern producers also stuff the tubes with ripe tea, and shops sell both. The tube is roasted over embers while the leaf is tamped and topped up, which steams the tea in the bamboo's own juice and gives a light toasty edge, then the bamboo is split away and the cylinder sold whole or sliced into coins.

In the cup, raw bamboo tea is honey and florals with a clear sweet-grassy bamboo fragrance and a touch of toast; the ripe version is dates and earth under the same bamboo sweetness. It is a gentle, likeable tea rather than a complex one. Break a coin into flakes along the layers, rinse twice and start with a longer steep; the cylinder is dense.

It is sold by the tube or by the coin, by year, with raw or ripe stated, from small producers in Xishuangbanna and Pu'er and from a handful of Western vendors who have it made. The tea inside is rarely premium, so pay for the craft and the aroma rather than for grand claims; a scorched, bitter bamboo tea was roasted too hard, a good one smells like a cut bamboo stalk. It also makes a handsome gift precisely because it looks like what it is.

It pairs naturally with Dai food, and a whole tube on a shelf is a conversation starter that happens to be drinkable.
history:
Tea packed into bamboo belongs to the village tea habits of southern Yunnan. Bamboo tube tea is counted among the characteristic teas of the Bulang people, next to their roasted and sour teas, and it is also a recognised, if uncommon, form of pu-erh, where the leaf is encased in bamboo and takes on smoke.

Little is documented about when the practice began or how it spread between peoples, so any claim about its age is best taken as local tradition. Today it survives both as a village product and as a small niche in the pu-erh trade.
